chunks: "There are two parts: seeing in all directions, and stitching what you see into a map. For the 360° coverage, the classic way is a spinning head.
A column of lasers and detectors, say 32 or 128 channels stacked vertically with different elevation angles, rotates around a vertical axis at 10 to 20 revolutions per second.
An encoder reports the azimuth at each firing, so each return has a range, an azimuth and a fixed elevation, and I convert that to x, y, z with sines and cosines.

Alternatives are a single laser with a rotating mirror for a 2D slice, MEMS or polygon mirrors for a limited field of view, or several solid-state units around the vehicle whose fields of view are stitched using a calibrated transform.
For the map: the sensor is moving, so one revolution of 100 milliseconds at 20 meters per second smears by 2 meters unless I correct it.
I use the IMU and wheel odometry to estimate the pose at each point's timestamp and transform every point into a common frame, called deskewing.
Then I register consecutive scans with ICP or NDT to estimate how the sensor moved and accumulate the points into a map.
Odometry drifts, so I use loop closure, recognizing a place I have seen before, and optimize the pose graph. That's LiDAR SLAM."
